title: Camino de Santiago
description: Pilgrimage routes to Santiago de Compostela, Spain
wiki_lead:
The Camino de Santiago (Latin: Peregrinatio Compostellana, lit. 'Pilgrimage of Compostela'; Galician: O Camiño de Santiago; Spanish: El Camino de Santiago; Portuguese: O Caminho de Santiago), or the Way of St. James in English, is a network of pilgrims' ways or pilgrimages leading to the shrine of the apostle James in the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia in northwestern Spain, where tradition holds that the remains of the apostle are buried. Pilgrims follow its routes as a form of spiritual path or retreat for their spiritual growth. It is also popular with hikers, cyclists, and organized tour groups.
Created and established in the beginning of the 9th century following the discovery of the relics of Saint James the Great, the Way of St. James became a major pilgrimage route of medieval Christianity from the 10th century onwards. Following the end of the  Granada War in 1492, under the reign of the Catholic Monarchs Ferdinand II of Aragon and Isabella I of Castile, Pope Alexander VI officially declared the Camino de Santiago to be one of the "three great pilgrimages of Christendom", along with Jerusalem and the Via Francigena to Rome.
In 1987, the Camino, which encompasses several routes in Spain, France, and Portugal, was declared the first Cultural Route of the Council of Europe. Since 2013, the Camino has attracted more than 200,000 pilgrims each year, with an annual growth rate of more than 10 percent. Pilgrims come mainly on foot and often from nearby cities, requiring several days of walking to reach Santiago. The French Way gathers two-thirds of the walkers, but other minor routes are experiencing a growth in popularity. The French Way and the Northern routes in Spain were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, followed by the routes in France in 1998, because of their historical significance for Christianity as a major pilgrimage route and their testimony to the exchange of ideas and cultures across the routes.

Major Christian pilgrimage route

The Way of St. James was one of the most important Christian pilgrimages during the later Middle Ages, and a pilgrimage route on which a plenary indulgence could be earned; other major pilgrimage routes include the Via Francigena to Rome and the pilgrimage to Jerusalem. Legend holds that St James's remains were carried by boat from Jerusalem to northern Spain, where he was buried in what is now the city of Santiago de Compostela (according to Spanish legends, Saint James had spent time preaching the gospel in Spain, but returned to Judaea upon seeing a vision of the Virgin Mary on the bank of the Ebro River).
Pilgrims on the Way can take one of dozens of pilgrimage routes to Santiago de Compostela. Traditionally, as with most pilgrimages, the Way of Saint James begins at one's home and ends at the pilgrimage site. However, a few of the routes are considered main ones. grok_lead: The Camino de Santiago, also known as the Way of Saint James, is a network of ancient Christian pilgrimage routes spanning Europe and converging at the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, northwestern Spain, believed to house the tomb of the apostle Saint James the Greater. Originating in the early 9th century after the reputed discovery of the saint's remains in 813 CE, it ranks as one of Christianity's three foremost pilgrimages, alongside those to Jerusalem and Rome, and has long symbolized spiritual journey, cultural exchange, and personal transformation. Pilgrims, or peregrinos, traditionally travel by foot, bicycle, or horseback, with the minimum requirement for official recognition being 100 kilometers walked or 200 kilometers cycled along a designated path, culminating in the issuance of the Compostela certificate by the Pilgrim's Reception Office in Santiago. The emblem of the pilgrimage is the scallop shell ( vieira), worn on clothing or backpacks to signify the pilgrim's status and the converging lines of the routes toward their shared destination, a tradition rooted in medieval practices where shells were distributed to returning pilgrims as proof of completion. The pilgrimage's historical foundations trace to the legend of Saint James evangelizing Iberia in the 1st century CE, with his body miraculously transported to Galicia after martyrdom in Jerusalem, though archaeological evidence supports the site's veneration from the 9th century onward. King Alfonso II of Asturias undertook the first documented pilgrimage in the early 9th century, establishing the Primitive Way from Oviedo, while the discovery prompted the construction of a chapel that evolved into the Romanesque cathedral, consecrated in 1211. The routes peaked in popularity during the 11th to 13th centuries, driven by royal patronage, the Reconquista, and monastic orders like the Knights Templar, who provided infrastructure such as bridges, hospitals, and hostels ( albergues), fostering a unique blend of Romanesque architecture, Gothic elements, and vernacular art along the paths. Designated as the first European Cultural Itinerary by the Council of Europe in 1987, the Camino's tangible heritageâencompassing over 200 monumentsâwas inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in phases: the old town of Santiago de Compostela in 1985 (ID 347), the French routes in 1998 (ID 868), the Camino FrancÃ©s and routes of northern Spain in 1993 (ID 669), with extensions to additional northern Spanish routes (Coastal, Interior, LiÃ©bana, and Primitive Ways, totaling about 1,500 km) in 2015 (ID 669). The most renowned route, the Camino FrancÃ©s, stretches approximately 780 km from Saint-Jean-Pied-de-Port in the French Pyrenees, crossing diverse landscapes from mountains to meseta plains, and passing UNESCO sites like the monasteries of San MillÃ¡n de la Cogolla and the cathedrals of Burgos and LeÃ³n. Other major paths include the Northern Way (about 825 km along the Cantabrian coast), the Portuguese Way (from Lisbon or Porto, around 620 km or 240 km respectively), the Primitive Way (from Oviedo, 320 km), and the Silver Way ( VÃ­a de la Plata, from Seville, 1,000 km), with over a dozen official variants recognized by the Federation of Associations of Friends of Saint James. Waymarking consists of yellow arrows and scallop shell motifs, a system formalized in the 1970s but echoing medieval signage, guiding pilgrims through rural villages, historic cities, and natural reserves while emphasizing the buen camino ethos of mutual support. In modern times, the Camino has experienced a resurgence since the 1980s, evolving from a primarily religious endeavor into a multifaceted experience attracting spiritual seekers, hikers, and cultural tourists; Holy Years ( AÃ±os Jacobeos), declared when July 25 falls on a Sunday, draw peak crowds, as in 2021â2022. Official statistics from the Pilgrim's Reception Office record 499,239 Compostelas issued in 2024, a 12% increase from 2023, with 85% of pilgrims arriving on foot, 4% by bike, and the remainder by horseback or other means; nationalities are diverse, led by Spaniards (43%), followed by Americans (8%), Italians (5%), Germans (5%), and Portuguese (4%). The most popular starting point is Sarria (30% of pilgrims), enabling the 100-km minimum, while the Camino FrancÃ©s accounts for over 60% of completions, underscoring its enduring appeal amid growing infrastructure like over 400 albergues and sustainable tourism initiatives by the Xunta de Galicia.
